subject: physics
title: Distance is not displacement
subtitle: Use a number line to distinguish where you finish from how far you traveled.
observe: A student walks across a room, turns around, and ends near the starting point. Can the distance traveled be large while the displacement is small?
idea: Position identifies an object's location relative to an origin. Displacement is final position minus initial position: Δx = xᶠ − xᶦ. Distance traveled counts the total length of the path and cannot be negative.
visualLead: Change where the cart turns and where it stops. Compare displacement, which includes direction, with total distance traveled.

example.question: A student starts at x = 1 m, walks to x = 7 m, then returns to x = 3 m. Find displacement and total distance.
steps: Displacement uses only the starting and ending positions: Δx = 3 − 1 = +2 m.
Distance traveled includes both segments: |7 − 1| + |3 − 7|.
Distance = 6 + 4 = 10 m. The student is only 2 m to the right of the starting point.

practice.prompt: A cart starts at 2 m, moves to 9 m, then ends at 5 m. What is the total distance traveled (in meters)?
hints: Count the distance along both legs of the journey, not just the displacement.

subject: physics
title: How can dots describe motion?
subtitle: Discover how equally spaced moments reveal speed and changes in speed.
observe: Suppose you saw only seven photographs of a moving cart, each taken at the same time interval. Could you tell whether it was speeding up?
idea: A motion diagram marks a body's position at equally spaced times. Equal distances between marks indicate constant speed; increasing distances indicate speeding up.
visualLead: Choose a pattern and replay the cart's motion. Notice the spacing between the dots.

example.question: A cart moves 12 meters over four equal one-second intervals, covering 3 meters in each. What is its average speed?
steps: Speed is the distance traveled divided by the elapsed time.
The cart travels 12 m in 4 s.
Average speed = 12 m / 4 s = 3 m/s. Equal intervals also show constant speed here.

practice.prompt: A cart travels 18 meters in 6 seconds. What is its average speed?
hints: Average speed compares distance with elapsed time.

subject: physics
title: Read velocity from a graph
subtitle: Use rise over run to connect a position–time graph with average velocity.
observe: Suppose two moving objects finish at the same position. Could one have a greater average velocity over a shorter interval?
idea: Average velocity over a time interval is displacement divided by elapsed time: v̄ = [x(t₂) − x(t₁)]/(t₂ − t₁). On a position–time graph, this is the slope of the secant line between the selected points.
visualLead: Drag the endpoints of a time interval across a curved position graph. Watch its average slope change.

example.question: An object has position x(t) = 1 + 2t + ¼t² meters. Find its average velocity from t = 0 to t = 4 seconds.
steps: Find the positions: x(0) = 1 m and x(4) = 1 + 8 + 4 = 13 m.
Displacement over the interval is 13 − 1 = 12 m. Elapsed time is 4 s.
Average velocity is 12/4 = 3 m/s. It is the slope of the line joining the two graph points.

practice.prompt: An object moves from x = 3 m at t = 1 s to x = 15 m at t = 5 s. What is its average velocity?
hints: Divide the change in position by the change in time.

subject: physics
title: When velocity changes
subtitle: Connect acceleration to the slope of a velocity–time graph.
observe: Can an object still move forward while accelerating backward? What would its velocity graph look like?
idea: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes: a = Δv/Δt. A negative acceleration describes a change toward the negative direction, not necessarily a slowing object.
visualLead: Adjust the acceleration. Watch the velocity–time graph and the prediction at t = 4 seconds.

example.question: A cart begins at 2 m/s and accelerates at 1.5 m/s² for 4 s. Find its final velocity.
steps: For constant acceleration, final velocity is initial velocity plus acceleration times time: v = v₀ + at.
Substitute v₀ = 2 m/s, a = 1.5 m/s², t = 4 s.
v = 2 + 1.5(4) = 8 m/s. Each second the velocity gains 1.5 m/s.

practice.prompt: A cart begins at 5 m/s and accelerates at −1 m/s² for 3 seconds. What is its final velocity?
hints: Use v = v₀ + at, keeping the negative acceleration.

subject: physics
title: Why does a falling object speed up?
subtitle: Predict the motion of an object released from rest under constant gravity.
observe: If an object is released from rest, does it fall the same distance during each successive second? Why not?
idea: When air resistance is negligible, the downward acceleration of a freely falling object is approximately constant near Earth's surface. Choosing up as positive gives y(t) = h − ½gt² and v(t) = −gt before impact.
visualLead: Move forward in time and compare a fall under Earth's gravity with one under the Moon's gravity. The model stops at impact.

example.question: A ball is dropped from rest 19.6 m above the ground. Ignoring air resistance, how long until it reaches the ground on Earth?
steps: Set vertical position to zero at impact: 0 = h − ½gt².
Use h = 19.6 m and g = 9.8 m/s²: 0 = 19.6 − 4.9t², so t² = 4.
The ball reaches the ground after t = 2 s. Its velocity immediately before impact is −19.6 m/s (up positive).

practice.prompt: An object is dropped from rest 44.1 m above the ground. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 9.8 m/s², how many seconds until impact?
hints: Use h = ½gt² for a drop from rest.

subject: physics
title: Three graphs tell one story
subtitle: See position, velocity and acceleration describe the same moving object.
observe: Could three different-looking graphs all describe one simple motion? What does the slope of each graph tell us?
idea: Position tells where an object is, velocity measures its rate of change of position, and acceleration measures its rate of change of velocity. For constant acceleration, x(t) = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² and v(t) = v₀ + at.
visualLead: Change the constant acceleration and choose a time. All three graphs describe the same motion. Notice how the slope of the position graph agrees with the velocity.

example.question: A cart starts at x₀ = 0 m with velocity 2 m/s, accelerating at 0.5 m/s². Where is it after 4 seconds?
steps: For constant acceleration, position is x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at².
Substitute the values: x = 0 + 2(4) + ½(0.5)(4²).
The result is x = 8 + 4 = 12 m. Its final velocity is 2 + 0.5(4) = 4 m/s.

practice.prompt: A cart begins at position 0 m with velocity 2 m/s and acceleration 1 m/s². What is its position after 2 seconds?

subject: calculus
title: The derivative is a changing slope
subtitle: See how a secant line approaches a tangent line.
observe: When a curve does not have a single constant slope, how can we determine how steep it is at one exact point?
idea: The derivative at x = a is the limit of nearby secant slopes. For f(x) = x², the average slope from a to a + h is 2a + h, approaching 2a as h approaches zero.
visualLead: Choose a point a, then decrease the distance h. Compare the secant slope with the tangent slope.

example.question: Find the slope of y = x² at x = 3 using the difference quotient.
steps: Start with [f(3+h) − f(3)] / h.
Expand: [(3+h)² − 9] / h = (6h + h²) / h.
For h ≠ 0 the expression is 6 + h. Its limit as h → 0 is 6.

practice.prompt: For f(x) = x², what is the derivative at x = −2?
hints: The derivative of x² at x is 2x.

subject: calculus
title: Area under velocity measures a journey
subtitle: Connect an integral to accumulated displacement and a changing physical quantity.
observe: If a graph tells you how fast an object is moving at each instant, how could you discover its overall change in position?
idea: Displacement is accumulated velocity. The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ v(t)dt gives net change in position, including the sign of velocity. When velocity stays positive, that integral also equals distance traveled.
visualLead: Extend the time interval under a changing velocity graph. See the shaded region and its accumulated displacement.

example.question: An object's velocity is v(t) = 3 + t meters per second. Find its displacement from t = 0 to t = 2 seconds.
steps: Displacement is the definite integral of velocity: Δx = ∫₀² (3+t) dt.
An antiderivative is 3t + ½t². Evaluate it from 0 to 2.
Δx = [6 + 2] − 0 = 8 m. The units are meters because (m/s)·s = m.

practice.prompt: For v(t) = 2 + t m/s, what is the displacement from t = 0 to t = 4 seconds?
hints: Find the area under a line with initial height 2 and final height 6.

subject: calculus
title: How rectangles discover area
subtitle: Understand a definite integral as the limit of sums.
observe: How could we estimate the area below a sloping line using only rectangles?
idea: A Riemann sum approximates an accumulated quantity by adding many small rectangular contributions. Refining the rectangles can make the approximation approach the exact definite integral.
visualLead: Increase the number of right-endpoint rectangles under y = x on [0,4]. Watch the excess area shrink.

example.question: Find the exact area under y = x from x = 0 to x = 4.
steps: A right-endpoint sum with n rectangles has Δx = 4/n.
As n increases without bound, the sum tends to 8 square units.

practice.prompt: What is the exact area under y = x from x = 0 to x = 6?
hints: For this straight line, the region is a triangle.
